title: MSVAE: Rethinking Musical Semantics in Continuous Latent Spaces

paper.title: MSVAE: Rethinking Musical Semantics in Continuous Latent Spaces
paper.abstract: Abstract Continuous latent representations underlie recent diffusion-based lyrics-to-song and text-to-music systems, yet aligning lyric conditions with these latents remains difficult: existing systems resort to generator-side machinery such as sentence-level timestamps, auxiliary alignment objectives, or semi-autoregressive decoding, while the latents they predict are still produced by autoencoders trained purely for reconstruction. We address this difficulty from the representation side. We propose MSVAE (Music Semantic Variational Autoencoder) 1 1 1 Demo, code, and weights: https://aslp-lab.github.io/MSVAE/ , which structures its continuous latent around two complementary semantic streams—work-level compositional content and lyric-level linguistic-vocal content. Partitioned dual-stream alignment makes both streams explicit by aligning disjoint latent subspaces with frozen lead-sheet and ASR references, while a semantic-first gated residual posterior derives its base from a frozen music-SSL encoder and admits acoustic information only through gated, bounded corrections. MSVAE achieves competitive stereo reconstruction and stronger MARBLE probing than continuous-autoencoder baselines, and improves downstream lyrics-to-song and text-to-music generation. Notably, with only an untimed phoneme prefix and no lyric timing, MSVAE yields the lowest phoneme error rate, whereas all baseline representations require sentence-level alignment to produce intelligible vocals.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Continuous latent representations have become a mainstream modeling space for recent diffusion-based generative models, including music generation models. Musical semantics encompass high-level melodic and harmonic organization as well as more explicit content relations such as lyric–vocal correspondence. Yet current continuous-latent systems struggle even with the latter: despite being directly observable and measurable, correspondence between lyric conditions and continuous latent sequences remains difficult to learn. Existing systems address this problem through auxiliary representation-alignment objectives, sentence-level temporal supervision, post-training rewards for alignment, and semi-autoregressive decoding ( Ning et al. 2025 ; Gong et al. 2025 ; Gong et al. 2026 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) . Despite their differences, all of these mechanisms are improvements on model design, while the target latents are mostly produced by autoencoders trained primarily for waveform reconstruction. Purely reconstruction-oriented training of music autoencoders preserves the rich acoustic detail required for waveform synthesis, but nothing in it ensures that content factors such as melody, harmony, and lyric-related linguistic information are organized in an explicit and predictable way in the latent space. As a result, the downstream generator must learn not only the latent distribution but also how these high-level content factors are organized within an acoustically oriented space, transferring substantial content-modeling pressure to the generator. Consistent with this, recent work in speech and general audio synthesis ( Niu et al. 2025 ; Dinkel et al. 2026 ; Yang et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2026 ; Yan et al. 2025 ; Li et al. 2026 ) uses semantic supervision or self-supervised encoder features to learn continuous audio latents. These studies show that semantic guidance can encourage more structured latent spaces that are better suited to downstream generation. This motivates addressing the difficulty from the representation side — designing a music semantic VAE whose latent supports high-fidelity reconstruction while explicitly structuring musical content. This raises a fundamental question: what constitutes musical semantics? Song-level semantic content comprises two primary, complementary streams: work-level compositional content, including melody and harmony, and lyric-level linguistic-vocal content ( Meseguer-Brocal et al. 2018 ) . The two semantic streams do not correspond to separate audio sources — vocal melody itself belongs to compositional content: a sung phrase carries melodic contour while simultaneously conveying phonetic content. ACE-Step reflects this distinction in practice: its REPA ( Yu et al. 2025 ) objective separately aligns the same DiT representation with MERT ( Li et al. 2024 ) and mHuBERT ( Boito et al. 2024 ) , drawing music- and speech-oriented semantic guidance in parallel. Yet the mHuBERT component is reduced to 0.01 during fine-tuning to avoid suppressing instrumental sounds ( Gong et al. 2025 ) , indicating that heterogeneous semantic objectives can interfere when imposed on an undivided representation. The first challenge is therefore to make both streams explicit within a compact latent without letting them interfere with each other. An SSL encoder does not explicitly distinguish the two streams defined above, but its output is already organized around content and therefore provides a more structured substrate for making the two streams explicit. At the same time, SSL features do not preserve all the acoustic information required for high-fidelity reconstruction. This motivates combining SSL-derived semantic structure with reconstruction-relevant acoustic information in a shared continuous latent. Without appropriate constraints, however, the reconstruction objective may dominate this fusion and make the latent depend primarily on the acoustic pathway, thereby weakening its semantic organization. The second challenge is therefore to construct a continuous music latent that preserves a clear and predictable semantic organization while retaining the acoustic detail required for high-fidelity reconstruction. To address these challenges, we propose MSVAE (Music Semantic Variational Autoencoder), built on partitioned dual-stream alignment and a semantic-first gated residual posterior. The partitioned objective aligns disjoint latent subspaces with representations from frozen SheetSage ( Donahue et al. 2022 ) and FireRedASR ( Xu et al. 2025 ) encoders, making compositional and linguistic-vocal content explicit while limiting interference between their supervision signals. The gated residual posterior derives its semantic base from a frozen MuQ ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) encoder and admits reconstruction-relevant acoustic information only through bounded residual corrections. MSVAE embeds explicit content organization within the VAE latent rather than leaving it entirely to the downstream generator. The main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose MSVAE, a Music Semantic VAE that addresses lyric–audio correspondence at the representation level by organizing compositional and linguistic-vocal content in separate latent subspaces. • We introduce a semantic-first gated residual posterior, which derives its semantic substrate from frozen MuQ features and integrates reconstruction-relevant acoustic details via bounded residual corrections. • MSVAE demonstrates competitive reconstruction, superior MARBLE probing, and improved downstream lyrics-to-song and text-to-music generation. Notably, it enables intelligible vocal synthesis from untimed phoneme prefixes without relying on sentence-level lyric timing.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text: Lyric alignment in song generation. Continuous-latent song generators have introduced a range of generator-side mechanisms for lyric alignment. DiffRhythm ( Ning et al. 2025 ) uses sentence-level timestamps during both training and inference. ACE-Step ( Gong et al. 2025 ) adds REPA ( Yu et al. 2025 ) objectives that align intermediate DiT features with MERT and mHuBERT representations, while ACE-Step 1.5 ( Gong et al. 2026 ) further applies reinforcement learning with an intrinsic reward derived from the consistency of its lyric–frame cross-attention maps. DiffRhythm 2 ( Jiang et al. 2025 ) adopts semi-autoregressive block flow matching, preserving parallel generation within each block while introducing autoregressive progression across blocks and thus giving up full-sequence parallelism. These mechanisms operate at the generator level and leave the autoencoder latent unchanged; MSVAE instead addresses lyric–audio correspondence at the representation level. Music-oriented continuous representations. Continuous representations for music generation have primarily served as high-fidelity reconstruction interfaces. Stable Audio Open ( Evans et al. 2025 ) and ACE-Step 1.5 ( Gong et al. 2026 ) employ convolutional VAEs optimized mainly for acoustic reconstruction, without imposing explicit semantic structure on the latent. SAME ( Parker et al. 2026 ) introduces semantic regularization into a Transformer-based music autoencoder, but its training data contain no vocal songs, and its objectives do not explicitly distinguish melodic–harmonic from lyric-related linguistic-vocal content. How to structure a reconstructive continuous latent around these music-specific semantic streams therefore remains unresolved. Figure 1: Overall architecture of our proposed MSVAE.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Given a stereo music waveform x ∈ ℝ 2 × L x\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times L} , MSVAE encodes it into a 64-dimensional stochastic continuous representation z ∈ ℝ T × 64 z\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 64} at 25 Hz. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , MSVAE combines partitioned dual-stream semantic alignment with a semantic-first gated residual posterior. The posterior derives its semantic base from features extracted by a frozen MuQ encoder and admits information from a trainable acoustic encoder only through bounded residual corrections whose contributions are gated by the projected MuQ features. A sample from the resulting posterior is decoded to reconstruct the input waveform. During training, z z is split into two 32-dimensional partitions, which are projected and aligned with representations from frozen SheetSage and FireRedASR encoders, corresponding to compositional melodic–harmonic and lyric-related linguistic-vocal content, respectively. The model is jointly trained with reconstruction and adversarial losses, KL regularization, and two stream-specific alignment objectives.

sections.heading: Partitioned Dual-Stream Semantic Alignment
sections.text: A complete song combines a singing voice with polyphonic accompaniment. Across these components, melody and harmony characterize composition-level musical content, while singing additionally carries phonetic and lexical information. We therefore operationalize song-level semantics as two complementary streams: compositional melodic–harmonic content and lyric-related linguistic-vocal content. This factorization concerns semantic content rather than isolated audio sources: a sung melody contributes to the compositional stream while simultaneously conveying linguistic content. To construct the compositional reference, we use hidden states from SheetSage’s separately trained melody-transcription and chord-recognition Transformers ( Donahue et al. 2022 ) . SheetSage is an audio-to-lead-sheet transcription system trained on approximately 50 hours of aligned melody and harmony annotations. Let H melody ∈ ℝ N × d melody , H harmony ∈ ℝ N × d harmony H^{\mathrm{melody}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\mathrm{melody}}},\qquad H^{\mathrm{harmony}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\mathrm{harmony}}} (1) denote its melody and harmony hidden sequences, respectively, where d melody + d harmony = 1024 d_{\mathrm{melody}}+d_{\mathrm{harmony}}=1024 in our implementation. Because these representations are indexed by beat-synchronous positions rather than a fixed frame rate, we expand them to the 25-Hz VAE grid by repeating each hidden vector in proportion to its duration, compensating for rounding errors to preserve sequence length. The expanded sequences are concatenated along the feature dimension to form the compositional reference H comp = [ H ~ harmony ∥ H ~ melody ] ∈ ℝ T × 1024 . H^{\mathrm{comp}}=[\widetilde{H}^{\mathrm{harmony}}\|\widetilde{H}^{\mathrm{melody}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1024}. (2) For the linguistic-vocal stream, we use the final encoder hidden states of a frozen FireRedASR-AED-L model ( Xu et al. 2025 ) . FireRedASR-AED-L uses a 16-layer Conformer encoder with a model width of 1280, followed by a Transformer decoder, and is trained for speech and singing transcription. Two stride-2 convolutional layers reduce its 10-ms input feature sequence to a nominal 40-ms frame interval. The resulting encoder representation H ling ∈ ℝ T × 1280 H^{\mathrm{ling}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1280} (3) therefore operates at approximately 25 Hz, allowing the corresponding segment to be selected without temporal interpolation. The trainable components of MSVAE are optimized jointly, while the MuQ, SheetSage, and FireRedASR encoders remain frozen. To complement the spectral reconstruction objectives, we employ the multi-period discriminator (MPD) and multi-resolution discriminator (MRD) used in DAC ( Kumar et al. 2023 ) , together with an MSS-CQT discriminator ( Gu et al. 2024 ) . We aggregate the generator-side adversarial and feature-matching losses produced by these discriminator families and denote them by ℒ adv \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}} and ℒ fm \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fm}} , respectively. The discriminators are optimized using their corresponding standard adversarial objectives, whose aggregate is denoted by ℒ D \mathcal{L}_{D} . Consistent with the latent partition used for semantic alignment, we regularize the corresponding marginals of the final gated residual posterior separately. sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.text: Training data and schedule. MSVAE is trained for 500k steps on approximately 600k vocal and instrumental tracks totaling about 40k hours, resampled to 24 kHz stereo, using random 4-second crops and a batch size of 32. We then freeze all other components and refine only the decoder for another 500k steps on approximately 300k tracks totaling about 20k hours, using 48-kHz reconstruction targets. Model configuration. MSVAE produces a 64-dimensional, 25-Hz latent using a DAC-style convolutional residual encoder ( Kumar et al. 2023 ) with 960 × 960\times downsampling and a BigVGAN-style decoder ( Lee et al. 2023 ) . MuQ processes the two stereo channels independently, and the MuQ, SheetSage, and FireRedASR encoders remain frozen. Complete implementation details are provided in the Appendix. Baselines and comparison protocol. We compare official checkpoints of Stable Audio Open ( Evans et al. 2025 ) and ACE-Step 1.5 ( Gong et al. 2026 ) , both convolutional VAEs, and the Transformer-based, semantically regularized SAME-S/L ( Parker et al. 2026 ) . Within each downstream task, all representations share the training data, generator architecture and scale, optimization schedule, and number of training steps; only the input/output projections and sequence lengths are adapted to their latent dimensions and frame rates. sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We evaluate music reconstruction on the official 50-track test split of MUSDB18-HQ ( Rafii et al. 2019 ) . We report four complementary metrics: PESQ ( Rix et al. 2001 ) and STOI ( Taal et al. 2010 ) emphasize perceptual quality and intelligibility ( Jiang et al. 2026 ) , whereas STFT log \mathrm{STFT}_{\log} and Mel log \mathrm{Mel}_{\log} measure spectral fidelity following the multi-resolution definitions of SAME ( Parker et al. 2026 ) . PESQ is computed in wideband mode at 16 kHz and STOI at 10 kHz; all metrics are computed per channel and averaged.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Within the 64-dimensional convolutional VAE block in Table 1 , MSVAE achieves the best PESQ and spectral distances, while its STOI is second only to ACE-Step 1.5. Explicit semantic organization is therefore compatible with competitive acoustic fidelity at a comparable latent and trainable-parameter budget. The SAME variants attain higher reconstruction scores but use a 1.7 × 1.7\times larger latent-rate budget. Both also undergo two encoder-frozen decoder-finetuning stages designed to improve reconstruction quality; SAME-L is substantially larger, while SAME-S is distilled from SAME-L.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We evaluate music understanding on selected tasks from the MARBLE benchmark ( Yuan et al. 2023 ) . All representation models are kept frozen, and only task-specific probing heads are trained under identical data splits and optimization settings. The selected tasks cover complementary aspects of musical content: EMO evaluates music emotion regression through the coefficients of determination R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} and R A 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{A}} for valence and arousal; Chords evaluates large-vocabulary chord recognition with accuracy; GS evaluates musical key detection on GiantSteps with weighted accuracy; and GTZAN Beat evaluates beat tracking with F1 score.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We evaluate each representation as the modeling space of a downstream generative model. Within each task, all representations use the same generator backbone and model scale, training data, optimization schedule, and number of training steps. For lyrics-to-song, we train a 1B non-autoregressive latent diffusion transformer following DiffRhythm+ ( Chen et al. 2025 ) on 200k songs at a training length of 45 seconds, and evaluate on 200 AI-generated lyrics. The generators built on the baseline representations follow the sentence-level alignment paradigm of DiffRhythm ( Ning et al. 2025 ) . For MSVAE, we train one generator with the same timestamped conditioning and another with an untimed phoneme-token prefix, the latter serving as our primary setting. Audiobox Aesthetics ( Tjandra et al. 2025 ) provides production quality (PQ) and content enjoyment (CE), while SongEval ( Yao et al. 2025 ) provides five song-level aesthetic dimensions. MuLan measures prompt–audio agreement in the MuQ-MuLan ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) embedding space, and phoneme error rate (PER) measures lyric intelligibility, computed on vocals separated by YingMusic-Singer ( Hao et al. 2026 ) and transcribed with Qwen3-ASR ( Qwen Team 2026 ) . For text-to-music, we follow the ICME2026 ATTM Grand Challenge protocol ( Hsieh et al. 2026 ) : a 400M conditional DiT based on DiffRhythm+ is trained on 30-second instrumental segments from MTG-Jamendo (3.7k hours) ( Bogdanov et al. 2019 ) and evaluated on the official test prompts. We report Fréchet audio distance (FAD) ( Kilgour et al. 2019 ) , CLAP score for text–audio alignment, and concept coverage score (CCS), which uses a large audio-language model to verify the presence of specified musical concepts.

sections.heading: Lyrics-to-Song
sections.text: As shown in Table 3 , the untimed MSVAE setting achieves the best CE, all five SongEval scores, and MuLan, with every SongEval dimension improving by more than 0.5 0.5 points over the strongest baseline representation. Despite receiving no explicit lyric timing, it attains a PER of 0.136 0.136 , lower than every timestamp-conditioned baseline. Providing MSVAE with sentence-level timestamps further reduces PER to 0.069 0.069 , but lowers CE, all five SongEval dimensions, and MuLan, revealing a trade-off between stronger lyric alignment and song-level quality; we therefore retain the untimed configuration as our primary setting. In contrast, when sentence-level alignment is replaced with an untimed prefix, vocals generated from every baseline representation no longer follow the supplied lyrics under the shared generator recipe (PER > 0.80 >0.80 ; Appendix). This timestamp-free capability extends beyond the 45-second setting. When trained from scratch at 90 and 150 seconds with the same untimed conditioning and no auxiliary generator-side alignment objective, MSVAE continues to produce intelligible vocals, with musicality remaining close to the 45-second setting although PER increases with duration (Appendix). These results indicate that the linguistic-vocal structure of the MSVAE latent substantially reduces reliance on externally specified lyric timing.

sections.heading: Ablation Studies
sections.text: All lyrics-to-song ablations in this section use an untimed phoneme prefix without the sentence-level alignment paradigm.

sections.heading: Semantic Alignment
sections.text: The upper block of Table 4 varies the alignment strategy under a fixed gated residual posterior. Reconstruction exhibits the clearest pattern: PESQ remains near 1.47 1.47 without alignment, under full-dimensional dual-stream alignment, or with either reference used alone, but rises to 2.253 2.253 when the lead-sheet and ASR references are assigned to disjoint subspaces. Thus, neither dual-reference alignment without partitioning nor either semantic stream alone is sufficient; their partitioned combination is required for the gated residual posterior to attain high-fidelity reconstruction. It is also the only alignment variant that produces a substantial reconstruction gain while remaining strong in both probing and generation. Replacing the lead-sheet reference with chroma also unlocks reconstruction and retains a low PER, but degrades probing and song musicality, showing that effective subspace allocation also depends on the semantic content of the references.

sections.heading: Posterior Design
sections.text: The lower block of Table 4 compares alternative ways of constructing the posterior. Without alignment, direct addition achieves the strongest reconstruction (PESQ 2.399 2.399 ), but its EMO R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} falls to 0.174 0.174 . By contrast, the unaligned gated residual posterior remains close to the MuQ-only variant ( 0.459 0.459 versus 0.476 0.476 ), indicating that gating prevents the acoustic branch from overriding the semantics inherited from MuQ. Partitioned alignment substantially restores the probing performance of direct addition, yet its musicality and PER remain markedly worse than those of the gated residual posterior, making the benefit of gating most evident in downstream generation. The MuQ-only and acoustic-only posteriors expose complementary limitations: the former retains strong probing and musicality but remains near a PESQ of 1.47 1.47 , whereas the latter provides reconstruction comparable to the full model but leaves the latent weakly structured, with an EMO R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} of only 0.152 0.152 in Table 5 . Complete reconstruction metrics for the acoustic-only variants are provided in the Appendix. By using MuQ as the posterior substrate and restricting the acoustic encoder to gated, bounded residual corrections, MSVAE combines these strengths, keeping reconstruction close to the strongest variants while attaining the best chord accuracy, PQ, and PER among the posterior-construction variants.

sections.heading: Representation-Side versus Generator-Side Guidance
sections.text: Table 5 compares where semantic guidance should be introduced while fixing the posterior architecture to a single acoustic encoder and removing sentence-level lyric timing. Without guidance, the downstream generator fails to align lyrics, yielding a PER of 1.394 1.394 . Generator-side REPA improves intelligibility, but MERT+mHuBERT leaves musicality unchanged, while Lead+ASR reduces PER to 0.198 0.198 at the cost of lowering musicality to 2.76 2.76 . Applying partitioned Lead+ASR alignment during VAE training instead achieves the best PQ, musicality, and PER among these controlled variants, while raising EMO R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} from 0.152 0.152 to 0.382 0.382 . This comparison shows that structuring semantics in the latent provides a more effective modeling space than injecting semantic guidance only during generator training.

sections.heading: Effect of the Linguistic Stream on Instrumental Music
sections.text: A natural concern is that the ASR-aligned stream may be detrimental when the target contains no linguistic-vocal content. Table 6 shows the opposite: relative to lead-sheet-only alignment, the partitioned dual-stream configuration reduces FAD from 0.662 0.662 to 0.547 0.547 while attaining the best CLAP and CCS. Neither single-stream variant consistently improves over no alignment. A plausible explanation is that constraining both halves encourages compositional content to remain localized in its designated subspace. With lead-sheet-only alignment, the remaining dimensions receive no stream-specific target and may still absorb melodic–harmonic variation. Retaining the ASR-aligned stream may therefore benefit instrumental generation by completing the partition-wise organization rather than by providing active linguistic content. sections.heading: Subspace Specialization
sections.text: We probe the two latent partitions by zeroing one half of z z before decoding. Retaining only the compositional partition reconstructs the accompaniment and renders the vocal melody as instrument-like humming, but produces no intelligible lyrics. Conversely, retaining only the linguistic-vocal partition preserves intelligible singing while reducing the accompaniment to sparse rhythmic backing. These complementary interventions indicate that partitioned alignment induces distinct functional roles for the two latent subspaces.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We presented MSVAE, a Music Semantic VAE that structures its continuous latent around two complementary semantic streams—compositional melodic–harmonic content and lyric-related linguistic-vocal content—by combining partitioned dual-stream alignment with a semantic-first gated residual posterior. Although motivated by the lyric–audio correspondence problem, this representation-side design yields broader benefits: competitive reconstruction, stronger semantic probing, and improved downstream generation for both sung and instrumental music, including intelligible singing for up to 150 seconds without sentence-level lyric timing. These results highlight semantically structured continuous latents as a promising foundation for music generation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations
sections.text: Our evaluation relies primarily on automated perceptual, semantic, transcription, and probing metrics, and we have not conducted a controlled human listening study. The downstream experiments use non-autoregressive conditional flow-matching transformers; whether the advantages of MSVAE transfer to autoregressive generators remains unverified. Stage II improves the decoder to synthesize 48-kHz audio while retaining a frozen encoder that operates on 24-kHz input. The resulting 48-kHz output should therefore be interpreted as decoder-side bandwidth refinement rather than evidence that the latent representation captures information above the encoder’s Nyquist frequency.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 arXiv:2610.17187v1 [eess.AS] 12 Oct 2026 MSVAE: Rethinking Musical Semantics in Continuous Latent Spaces Guobin Ma Yuepeng Jiang Dake Guo Huakang Chen Yuan Zhou Lingxin Xiong Wenkai Cheng Jingbin Hu Hanke Xie Chunbo Hao Wenhao Li Ziqian Ning Jixun Yao Jian Zhao Zhonglin Jiang Yong Chen Lei Xie Pengcheng Zhu Abstract Continuous latent representations underlie recent diffusion-based lyrics-to-song and text-to-music systems, yet aligning lyric conditions with these latents remains difficult: existing systems resort to generator-side machinery such as sentence-level timestamps, auxiliary alignment objectives, or semi-autoregressive decoding, while the latents they predict are still produced by autoencoders trained purely for reconstruction. We address this difficulty from the representation side. We propose MSVAE (Music Semantic Variational Autoencoder) 1 1 1 Demo, code, and weights: https://aslp-lab.github.io/MSVAE/ , which structures its continuous latent around two complementary semantic streams—work-level compositional content and lyric-level linguistic-vocal content. Partitioned dual-stream alignment makes both streams explicit by aligning disjoint latent subspaces with frozen lead-sheet and ASR references, while a semantic-first gated residual posterior derives its base from a frozen music-SSL encoder and admits acoustic information only through gated, bounded corrections. MSVAE achieves competitive stereo reconstruction and stronger MARBLE probing than continuous-autoencoder baselines, and improves downstream lyrics-to-song and text-to-music generation. Notably, with only an untimed phoneme prefix and no lyric timing, MSVAE yields the lowest phoneme error rate, whereas all baseline representations require sentence-level alignment to produce intelligible vocals. 1 Audio, Speech and Language Processing Group (ASLP@NPU), School of Software, Northwestern Polytechnical University, China 2 Geely Automobile Research Institute (Ningbo) Company Ltd, China 3 Independent Researcher, China 4 Faculty of Electronic and Information Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University, China 5 WeNet Open Source Community, China guobin.ma@mail.nwpu.edu.cn, lxie@nwpu.edu.cn, zpcoftts@gmail.com Introduction Continuous latent representations have become a mainstream modeling space for recent diffusion-based generative models, including music generation models. Musical semantics encompass high-level melodic and harmonic organization as well as more explicit content relations such as lyric–vocal correspondence. Yet current continuous-latent systems struggle even with the latter: despite being directly observable and measurable, correspondence between lyric conditions and continuous latent sequences remains difficult to learn. Existing systems address this problem through auxiliary representation-alignment objectives, sentence-level temporal supervision, post-training rewards for alignment, and semi-autoregressive decoding ( Ning et al. 2025 ; Gong et al. 2025 ; Gong et al. 2026 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) . Despite their differences, all of these mechanisms are improvements on model design, while the target latents are mostly produced by autoencoders trained primarily for waveform reconstruction. Purely reconstruction-oriented training of music autoencoders preserves the rich acoustic detail required for waveform synthesis, but nothing in it ensures that content factors such as melody, harmony, and lyric-related linguistic information are organized in an explicit and predictable way in the latent space. As a result, the downstream generator must learn not only the latent distribution but also how these high-level content factors are organized within an acoustically oriented space, transferring substantial content-modeling pressure to the generator. Consistent with this, recent work in speech and general audio synthesis ( Niu et al. 2025 ; Dinkel et al. 2026 ; Yang et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2026 ; Yan et al. 2025 ; Li et al. 2026 ) uses semantic supervision or self-supervised encoder features to learn continuous audio latents. These studies show that semantic guidance can encourage more structured latent spaces that are better suited to downstream generation. This motivates addressing the difficulty from the representation side — designing a music semantic VAE whose latent supports high-fidelity reconstruction while explicitly structuring musical content. This raises a fundamental question: what constitutes musical semantics? Song-level semantic content comprises two primary, complementary streams: work-level compositional content, including melody and harmony, and lyric-level linguistic-vocal content ( Meseguer-Brocal et al. 2018 ) . The two semantic streams do not correspond to separate audio sources — vocal melody itself belongs to compositional content: a sung phrase carries melodic contour while simultaneously conveying phonetic content. ACE-Step reflects this distinction in practice: its REPA ( Yu et al. 2025 ) objective separately aligns the same DiT representation with MERT ( Li et al. 2024 ) and mHuBERT ( Boito et al. 2024 ) , drawing music- and speech-oriented semantic guidance in parallel. Yet the mHuBERT component is reduced to 0.01 during fine-tuning to avoid suppressing instrumental sounds ( Gong et al. 2025 ) , indicating that heterogeneous semantic objectives can interfere when imposed on an undivided representation. The first challenge is therefore to make both streams explicit within a compact latent without letting them interfere with each other. An SSL encoder does not explicitly distinguish the two streams defined above, but its output is already organized around content and therefore provides a more structured substrate for making the two streams explicit. At the same time, SSL features do not preserve all the acoustic information required for high-fidelity reconstruction. This motivates combining SSL-derived semantic structure with reconstruction-relevant acoustic information in a shared continuous latent. Without appropriate constraints, however, the reconstruction objective may dominate this fusion and make the latent depend primarily on the acoustic pathway, thereby weakening its semantic organization. The second challenge is therefore to construct a continuous music latent that preserves a clear and predictable semantic organization while retaining the acoustic detail required for high-fidelity reconstruction. To address these challenges, we propose MSVAE (Music Semantic Variational Autoencoder), built on partitioned dual-stream alignment and a semantic-first gated residual posterior. The partitioned objective aligns disjoint latent subspaces with representations from frozen SheetSage ( Donahue et al. 2022 ) and FireRedASR ( Xu et al. 2025 ) encoders, making compositional and linguistic-vocal content explicit while limiting interference between their supervision signals. The gated residual posterior derives its semantic base from a frozen MuQ ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) encoder and admits reconstruction-relevant acoustic information only through bounded residual corrections. MSVAE embeds explicit content organization within the VAE latent rather than leaving it entirely to the downstream generator. The main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose MSVAE, a Music Semantic VAE that addresses lyric–audio correspondence at the representation level by organizing compositional and linguistic-vocal content in separate latent subspaces. • We introduce a semantic-first gated residual posterior, which derives its semantic substrate from frozen MuQ features and integrates reconstruction-relevant acoustic details via bounded residual corrections. • MSVAE demonstrates competitive reconstruction, superior MARBLE probing, and improved downstream lyrics-to-song and text-to-music generation. Notably, it enables intelligible vocal synthesis from untimed phoneme prefixes without relying on sentence-level lyric timing. Related Work Lyric alignment in song generation. Continuous-latent song generators have introduced a range of generator-side mechanisms for lyric alignment. DiffRhythm ( Ning et al. 2025 ) uses sentence-level timestamps during both training and inference. ACE-Step ( Gong et al. 2025 ) adds REPA ( Yu et al. 2025 ) objectives that align intermediate DiT features with MERT and mHuBERT representations, while ACE-Step 1.5 ( Gong et al. 2026 ) further applies reinforcement learning with an intrinsic reward derived from the consistency of its lyric–frame cross-attention maps. DiffRhythm 2 ( Jiang et al. 2025 ) adopts semi-autoregressive block flow matching, preserving parallel generation within each block while introducing autoregressive progression across blocks and thus giving up full-sequence parallelism. These mechanisms operate at the generator level and leave the autoencoder latent unchanged; MSVAE instead addresses lyric–audio correspondence at the representation level. Music-oriented continuous representations. Continuous representations for music generation have primarily served as high-fidelity reconstruction interfaces. Stable Audio Open ( Evans et al. 2025 ) and ACE-Step 1.5 ( Gong et al. 2026 ) employ convolutional VAEs optimized mainly for acoustic reconstruction, without imposing explicit semantic structure on the latent. SAME ( Parker et al. 2026 ) introduces semantic regularization into a Transformer-based music autoencoder, but its training data contain no vocal songs, and its objectives do not explicitly distinguish melodic–harmonic from lyric-related linguistic-vocal content. How to structure a reconstructive continuous latent around these music-specific semantic streams therefore remains unresolved. Figure 1: Overall architecture of our proposed MSVAE. Methodology Overview Given a stereo music waveform x ∈ ℝ 2 × L x\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times L} , MSVAE encodes it into a 64-dimensional stochastic continuous representation z ∈ ℝ T × 64 z\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 64} at 25 Hz. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , MSVAE combines partitioned dual-stream semantic alignment with a semantic-first gated residual posterior. The posterior derives its semantic base from features extracted by a frozen MuQ encoder and admits information from a trainable acoustic encoder only through bounded residual corrections whose contributions are gated by the projected MuQ features. A sample from the resulting posterior is decoded to reconstruct the input waveform. During training, z z is split into two 32-dimensional partitions, which are projected and aligned with representations from frozen SheetSage and FireRedASR encoders, corresponding to compositional melodic–harmonic and lyric-related linguistic-vocal content, respectively. The model is jointly trained with reconstruction and adversarial losses, KL regularization, and two stream-specific alignment objectives. Partitioned Dual-Stream Semantic Alignment A complete song combines a singing voice with polyphonic accompaniment. Across these components, melody and harmony characterize composition-level musical content, while singing additionally carries phonetic and lexical information. We therefore operationalize song-level semantics as two complementary streams: compositional melodic–harmonic content and lyric-related linguistic-vocal content. This factorization concerns semantic content rather than isolated audio sources: a sung melody contributes to the compositional stream while simultaneously conveying linguistic content. To construct the compositional reference, we use hidden states from SheetSage’s separately trained melody-transcription and chord-recognition Transformers ( Donahue et al. 2022 ) . SheetSage is an audio-to-lead-sheet transcription system trained on approximately 50 hours of aligned melody and harmony annotations. Because these representations are indexed by beat-synchronous positions rather than a fixed frame rate, we expand them to the 25-Hz VAE grid by repeating each hidden vector in proportion to its duration, compensating for rounding errors to preserve sequence length. The expanded sequences are concatenated along the feature dimension to form the compositional reference H comp = [ H ~ harmony ∥ H ~ melody ] ∈ ℝ T × 1024 . H^{\mathrm{comp}}=[\widetilde{H}^{\mathrm{harmony}}\|\widetilde{H}^{\mathrm{melody}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1024}. FireRedASR-AED-L uses a 16-layer Conformer encoder with a model width of 1280, followed by a Transformer decoder, and is trained for speech and singing transcription. Two stride-2 convolutional layers reduce its 10-ms input feature sequence to a nominal 40-ms frame interval. The resulting encoder representation H ling ∈ ℝ T × 1280 H^{\mathrm{ling}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1280} (3) therefore operates at approximately 25 Hz, allowing the corresponding segment to be selected without temporal interpolation. MSVAE is trained for 500k steps on approximately 600k vocal and instrumental tracks totaling about 40k hours, resampled to 24 kHz stereo, using random 4-second crops and a batch size of 32. We then freeze all other components and refine only the decoder for another 500k steps on approximately 300k tracks totaling about 20k hours, using 48-kHz reconstruction targets. Model configuration. MSVAE produces a 64-dimensional, 25-Hz latent using a DAC-style convolutional residual encoder ( Kumar et al. 2023 ) with 960 × 960\times downsampling and a BigVGAN-style decoder ( Lee et al. 2023 ) . MuQ processes the two stereo channels independently, and the MuQ, SheetSage, and FireRedASR encoders remain frozen. Complete implementation details are provided in the Appendix. Baselines and comparison protocol. We report four complementary metrics: PESQ ( Rix et al. 2001 ) and STOI ( Taal et al. 2010 ) emphasize perceptual quality and intelligibility ( Jiang et al. 2026 ) , whereas STFT log \mathrm{STFT}_{\log} and Mel log \mathrm{Mel}_{\log} measure spectral fidelity following the multi-resolution definitions of SAME ( Parker et al. 2026 ) . Results Within the 64-dimensional convolutional VAE block in Table 1 , MSVAE achieves the best PESQ and spectral distances, while its STOI is second only to ACE-Step 1.5. Explicit semantic organization is therefore compatible with competitive acoustic fidelity at a comparable latent and trainable-parameter budget. The SAME variants attain higher reconstruction scores but use a 1.7 × 1.7\times larger latent-rate budget. Both also undergo two encoder-frozen decoder-finetuning stages designed to improve reconstruction quality; SAME-L is substantially larger, while SAME-S is distilled from SAME-L. Music Understanding Setup We evaluate music understanding on selected tasks from the MARBLE benchmark ( Yuan et al. 2023 ) . All representation models are kept frozen, and only task-specific probing heads are trained under identical data splits and optimization settings. The selected tasks cover complementary aspects of musical content: EMO evaluates music emotion regression through the coefficients of determination R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} and R A 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{A}} for valence and arousal; Chords evaluates large-vocabulary chord recognition with accuracy; GS evaluates musical key detection on GiantSteps with weighted accuracy; and GTZAN Beat evaluates beat tracking with F1 score. Results Table 2 shows that MSVAE outperforms all continuous-autoencoder baselines across the five reported metrics. The largest gain appears in valence regression, where R V 2 R_{V}^{2} increases from 0.267 0.267 to 0.469 0.469 ; clear gains are also observed in chord recognition and beat tracking. Despite using only a 64-dimensional latent at 25 Hz and additionally supporting waveform decoding, MSVAE surpasses the 1024-dimensional SheetSage reference on four of the five metrics and MuQ layer 6 on key estimation. These results demonstrate that MSVAE preserves substantial musical semantic information within a compact, reconstructive latent representation. Downstream Music Generation Setup We evaluate each representation as the modeling space of a downstream generative model. Within each task, all representations use the same generator backbone and model scale, training data, optimization schedule, and number of training steps. For lyrics-to-song, we train a 1B non-autoregressive latent diffusion transformer following DiffRhythm+ ( Chen et al. 2025 ) on 200k songs at a training length of 45 seconds, and evaluate on 200 AI-generated lyrics. The generators built on the baseline representations follow the sentence-level alignment paradigm of DiffRhythm ( Ning et al. 2025 ) . For MSVAE, we train one generator with the same timestamped conditioning and another with an untimed phoneme-token prefix, the latter serving as our primary setting. Audiobox Aesthetics ( Tjandra et al. 2025 ) provides production quality (PQ) and content enjoyment (CE), while SongEval ( Yao et al. 2025 ) provides five song-level aesthetic dimensions. MuLan measures prompt–audio agreement in the MuQ-MuLan ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) embedding space, and phoneme error rate (PER) measures lyric intelligibility, computed on vocals separated by YingMusic-Singer ( Hao et al. 2026 ) and transcribed with Qwen3-ASR ( Qwen Team 2026 ) . For text-to-music, we follow the ICME2026 ATTM Grand Challenge protocol ( Hsieh et al. 2026 ) : a 400M conditional DiT based on DiffRhythm+ is trained on 30-second instrumental segments from MTG-Jamendo (3.7k hours) ( Bogdanov et al. 2019 ) and evaluated on the official test prompts. We report Fréchet audio distance (FAD) ( Kilgour et al. 2019 ) , CLAP score for text–audio alignment, and concept coverage score (CCS), which uses a large audio-language model to verify the presence of specified musical concepts. Lyrics-to-Song As shown in Table 3 , the untimed MSVAE setting achieves the best CE, all five SongEval scores, and MuLan, with every SongEval dimension improving by more than 0.5 0.5 points over the strongest baseline representation. Despite receiving no explicit lyric timing, it attains a PER of 0.136 0.136 , lower than every timestamp-conditioned baseline. Providing MSVAE with sentence-level timestamps further reduces PER to 0.069 0.069 , but lowers CE, all five SongEval dimensions, and MuLan, revealing a trade-off between stronger lyric alignment and song-level quality; we therefore retain the untimed configuration as our primary setting. In contrast, when sentence-level alignment is replaced with an untimed prefix, vocals generated from every baseline representation no longer follow the supplied lyrics under the shared generator recipe (PER > 0.80 >0.80 ; Appendix). This timestamp-free capability extends beyond the 45-second setting. When trained from scratch at 90 and 150 seconds with the same untimed conditioning and no auxiliary generator-side alignment objective, MSVAE continues to produce intelligible vocals, with musicality remaining close to the 45-second setting although PER increases with duration (Appendix). These results indicate that the linguistic-vocal structure of the MSVAE latent substantially reduces reliance on externally specified lyric timing. Text-to-Music MSVAE also achieves the strongest overall performance on text-to-music generation, reducing FAD from the best baseline result of 0.660 0.660 to 0.547 0.547 and improving CCS from 0.698 0.698 to 0.735 0.735 . These improvements indicate better distributional quality and more reliable realization of the musical concepts specified by the prompt. Its CLAP score remains competitive, although slightly below those of the two SAME variants. This is expected, as SAME-L is trained with a cross-modal contrastive objective that explicitly aligns its latent with caption embeddings, and SAME-S inherits this property through distillation from SAME-L. MSVAE attains its FAD and CCS improvements without an audio–caption alignment objective during VAE training. Ablation Studies All lyrics-to-song ablations in this section use an untimed phoneme prefix without the sentence-level alignment paradigm. Semantic Alignment The upper block of Table 4 varies the alignment strategy under a fixed gated residual posterior. Reconstruction exhibits the clearest pattern: PESQ remains near 1.47 1.47 without alignment, under full-dimensional dual-stream alignment, or with either reference used alone, but rises to 2.253 2.253 when the lead-sheet and ASR references are assigned to disjoint subspaces. Thus, neither dual-reference alignment without partitioning nor either semantic stream alone is sufficient; their partitioned combination is required for the gated residual posterior to attain high-fidelity reconstruction. It is also the only alignment variant that produces a substantial reconstruction gain while remaining strong in both probing and generation. Replacing the lead-sheet reference with chroma also unlocks reconstruction and retains a low PER, but degrades probing and song musicality, showing that effective subspace allocation also depends on the semantic content of the references. Posterior Design The lower block of Table 4 compares alternative ways of constructing the posterior. Without alignment, direct addition achieves the strongest reconstruction (PESQ 2.399 2.399 ), but its EMO R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} falls to 0.174 0.174 . By contrast, the unaligned gated residual posterior remains close to the MuQ-only variant ( 0.459 0.459 versus 0.476 0.476 ), indicating that gating prevents the acoustic branch from overriding the semantics inherited from MuQ. Partitioned alignment substantially restores the probing performance of direct addition, yet its musicality and PER remain markedly worse than those of the gated residual posterior, making the benefit of gating most evident in downstream generation. The MuQ-only and acoustic-only posteriors expose complementary limitations: the former retains strong probing and musicality but remains near a PESQ of 1.47 1.47 , whereas the latter provides reconstruction comparable to the full model but leaves the latent weakly structured, with an EMO R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} of only 0.152 0.152 in Table 5 . Complete reconstruction metrics for the acoustic-only variants are provided in the Appendix. By using MuQ as the posterior substrate and restricting the acoustic encoder to gated, bounded residual corrections, MSVAE combines these strengths, keeping reconstruction close to the strongest variants while attaining the best chord accuracy, PQ, and PER among the posterior-construction variants. Representation-Side versus Generator-Side Guidance Table 5 compares where semantic guidance should be introduced while fixing the posterior architecture to a single acoustic encoder and removing sentence-level lyric timing. Without guidance, the downstream generator fails to align lyrics, yielding a PER of 1.394 1.394 . Generator-side REPA improves intelligibility, but MERT+mHuBERT leaves musicality unchanged, while Lead+ASR reduces PER to 0.198 0.198 at the cost of lowering musicality to 2.76 2.76 . Applying partitioned Lead+ASR alignment during VAE training instead achieves the best PQ, musicality, and PER among these controlled variants, while raising EMO R V 2 R^{2}_{\mathrm{V}} from 0.152 0.152 to 0.382 0.382 . This comparison shows that structuring semantics in the latent provides a more effective modeling space than injecting semantic guidance only during generator training. Effect of the Linguistic Stream on Instrumental Music A natural concern is that the ASR-aligned stream may be detrimental when the target contains no linguistic-vocal content. Table 6 shows the opposite: relative to lead-sheet-only alignment, the partitioned dual-stream configuration reduces FAD from 0.662 0.662 to 0.547 0.547 while attaining the best CLAP and CCS. Neither single-stream variant consistently improves over no alignment. A plausible explanation is that constraining both halves encourages compositional content to remain localized in its designated subspace. With lead-sheet-only alignment, the remaining dimensions receive no stream-specific target and may still absorb melodic–harmonic variation. Retaining the ASR-aligned stream may therefore benefit instrumental generation by completing the partition-wise organization rather than by providing active linguistic content.
